scenes.sub: Construct an object in memory you already have.
scenes.say: Placement new. Normal new does two jobs: it allocates memory, and it constructs an object there. Placement new does only the second job.

scenes.head: Construct without allocating

items.label: buf: raw bytes on the stack

scenes.say: First we reserve raw bytes, sized and aligned for a Point. No object exists yet. Then new, with buf in parentheses, allocates nothing. It just runs the constructor at that address, and returns a pointer to the new object. When we're done, we call the destructor ourselves, explicitly. And we never call delete on p, because delete would try to free memory that new never allocated.

scenes.head: The destructor is your job
scenes.say: Here's proof that cleanup is your job. Placement new prints ctor. The explicit destructor call prints dtor. Leave that line out, and dtor never prints. The buffer just goes away, and any resource the object held, like a file or heap memory, leaks. Also, the buffer must be big enough and correctly aligned, or you get undefined behavior.

scenes.head: Where it's used
scenes.say: Where is it used? Vector reserves raw capacity, then constructs each element in place as you push back. Optional keeps raw storage inside itself, and constructs the value only when you set it. And memory pools grab one big block, then place many objects inside it. Since C plus plus twenty, s t d colon colon construct at does the same job, and also works in constexpr code.

lines: Placement new constructs an object at an address you provide. No allocation.
You must call the destructor yourself, and never delete it.
Memory must be big enough and aligned. Used inside vector, optional, pools.
